questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish internal from external validity in a pilot claim
questions.stem: A city pilot of a low-traffic street scheme runs in one neighbourhood and the memo presents the results as evidence for the whole city.

options.text: The pilot has internal validity for that street but weak external validity, since one neighbourhood may not represent the city.
The pilot has external validity because the scheme was implemented exactly as the city intended.
options.misconception: Treats faithful implementation as proof of generalisability

options.text: The pilot has internal validity because the intervention was delivered by trained city staff.
options.misconception: Treats trained delivery as evidence about other neighbourhoods

options.text: The pilot has neither validity because results from a single neighbourhood are never usable.
options.misconception: Believes a single site can never support any inference

questions.explanation: Internal validity is about cause in that setting, external validity about extension elsewhere. One neighbourhood may differ in traffic and retail mix, so the city-wide claim is unsupported.
questions.hint: Cause in place, and extension beyond place.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read a p value and sample size against a memo's claim
questions.stem: A memo reports that a pilot cut bus delays by 4 minutes with a p value of 0.42 and a sample of 12 buses; the council plans to publish it as a proven saving.

options.text: With a p value of 0.42 and twelve buses, the data are compatible with no effect, so the saving is not established.
A positive effect estimate is enough to publish the saving, because the point estimate shows the direction clearly.
options.misconception: Treats a point estimate as a proven effect

options.text: The p value of 0.42 is close to the conventional threshold, so the result is borderline and should be published.
options.misconception: Misreads 0.42 as near the significance threshold

options.text: Twelve buses is enough for a pilot, since pilot work does not require the same precision as a full scheme.
options.misconception: Waives precision requirements for pilot work

questions.explanation: A p value of 0.42 means the data are compatible with no difference, so the 4 minutes could be chance. Statistical conclusion validity requires ruling out chance before the claim is published.
questions.hint: A large p value means the effect is not established.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how attrition changes who remains in a study
questions.stem: A housing consultation had 900 responses in week one and 300 by the closing date after many participants moved or withdrew.

answer.exemplar: Attrition is the loss of participants between waves or between the start and the end of a study, and here 600 of the original 900 are missing. If those who dropped out differ systematically from those who stayed, the remaining 300 responses are not simply a smaller version of the original group but a differently composed one, and any trend computed on them may reflect who left rather than what changed.

questions.explanation: Attrition changes who remains, not just how many. If those who withdrew differ from those who stayed, the final responses are a differently composed group and trends drawn from them may reflect the withdrawals.
questions.hint: Ask who is missing, not just how many.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of respondents who would use a scheme
questions.stem: A bike lane consultation recruits 400 people at a park entrance; of them 260 say they would use the lane, and 140 say they would not. What percentage of respondents would use it?
questions.explanation: The share that would use the lane is 260 divided by 400, which is 65 percent. Recruiting at a park entrance shapes the denominator, so the arithmetic is right but the group is not random.
questions.hint: Divide the users by all respondents recruited.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order steps that separate a scheme from world events
questions.stem: A city wants to know whether a new lighting scheme reduces night-time collisions; put the steps in the order that separates the scheme from world events.

options.text: Collect before and after collision counts across comparable untreated streets, then check that no other policy changed.
Compare the treated street with itself before and after the scheme, because the same street controls for everything.
options.misconception: Assumes a single street controls for outside events

options.text: Compare collision counts after the scheme with the previous year's figures, since the year before is the natural baseline.
options.misconception: Uses a year-on-year baseline that shares the history

options.text: Collect counts from untreated streets only, since untouched streets show what would have happened anyway.
options.misconception: Ignores the treated street when estimating the trend

questions.explanation: A history effect occurs when an outside event changes the outcome, and untreated comparison streets reveal whether one coincided. Comparing a treated street with itself cannot separate scheme from city-wide change.
questions.hint: You need an untreated comparison for history.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a waiting list comparison contributes

stimulus.body: Programme note for a youth sports scheme. Coaches recorded self-reported confidence scores for 60 young people at the start of the twelve-week programme, at week six and again at week twelve. A separate group of 60 young people who joined a waiting list were measured on exactly the same dates using the same questionnaire.

questions.stem: Using the programme note above, why does the waiting list comparison strengthen the reading of the confidence scores?

options.text: The waiting list shows how confidence changes with time alone, so programme growth above that is attributable to the scheme.
The waiting list doubles the sample size, which narrows the error bars around the programme scores.
options.misconception: Believes a larger sample is the main benefit of a control group

options.text: The waiting list confirms the questionnaire is reliable because the same measure was used twice.
options.misconception: Treats repeated measurement as evidence of reliability

options.text: The waiting list shows the scheme has no effect, since the waiters improved at the same rate.
options.misconception: Assumes equal growth proves the scheme did nothing

questions.explanation: Maturation is change over time regardless of treatment, so a waiting list group measures that trajectory. Programme growth beyond the waiting list's growth can then be attributed to the scheme.
questions.hint: Waiting list groups track change over time.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the design that estimates a testing effect
questions.stem: A memo reports that residents who took a traffic questionnaire scored lower wellbeing than those who did not; a retest is planned. Which step comes first?

options.text: Re-test a comparable group who took the questionnaire earlier, so repeat exposure effects can be estimated.
Re-test the same residents who took the questionnaire, since only they can show change over time.
options.misconception: Re-tests the exposed group and repeats the same design flaw

options.text: Compare the questionnaire group's wellbeing with a published city average, so the comparison is quick.
options.misconception: Compares with an unknown population rather than a control group

options.text: Re-test the residents who did not take the questionnaire, so the original difference can be confirmed.
options.misconception: Chooses a comparison group with no exposure at all

questions.explanation: A testing effect means the measurement changes later responses, so a comparable group already exposed to the questionnaire must be re-tested. Re-testing the same residents or citing a city average cannot estimate it.
questions.hint: Compare with people already exposed to the test.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why extreme first readings drift downward
questions.stem: A clinic offers a follow-up programme to patients whose first blood pressure reading was extremely high, and their second reading falls.

options.text: Extremely high first readings are partly noise, so later readings drift downward regardless of the programme.
The fall proves the programme works, since the patients were selected because their readings were high.
options.misconception: Ignores regression to the mean in the selection rule

options.text: The fall shows the clinic's measurement protocol was inconsistent between the two visits.
options.misconception: Blames measurement error instead of statistical regression

options.text: The fall is evidence against the programme, since the patients did not improve as expected.
options.misconception: Reads a mean reversion as proof of harm

questions.explanation: Regression to the mean occurs when extreme first readings are partly chance, so later readings drift toward the average. The fall would appear without the programme, so selecting on extreme values confounds the effect.
questions.hint: Extreme first scores drift back on their own.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read a pilot result against a city-wide proposal
questions.stem: A bus lane in one ward cut car journeys by 12 percent and the memo proposes it for twelve wards without checking their travel patterns.

options.text: Internal validity in the pilot ward does not transfer, because other wards may have different road layouts and demand.
External validity follows from the size of the effect, since a 12 percent reduction is large enough to generalise.
options.misconception: Treats effect size as the basis for generalisation

options.text: Internal validity holds city-wide, because the pilot used the same signal timings as the rest of the city.
options.misconception: Assumes matching signals transfers findings to all wards

options.text: External validity is settled once the pilot scheme was carried out under normal council rules.
options.misconception: Equates normal implementation with generalisability

questions.explanation: Internal validity concerns cause in the pilot ward, external validity extension to others. A 12 percent effect in one ward says little about layouts and demand elsewhere, and identical timings do not close that gap.
questions.hint: One ward's cause, other wards' conditions.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a short series lacks a sound conclusion
questions.stem: A planning memo claims a new park increased footfall by 9 percent based on 8 days of counter readings and no comparison site.

answer.exemplar: Without a comparison site, the readings cannot distinguish the park from anything else that changed in those eight days, such as a nearby road closure or a school holiday, so the conclusion is not statistically sound even if the counter is accurate. A longer series with a matched untreated location would let the memo say whether the park produced an increase rather than whether footfall happened to rise at the same time.

questions.explanation: Statistical conclusion validity requires evidence that rules out chance and alternatives. Eight days without a comparison site cannot do that, and simply collecting more of the same readings would not fix it.
questions.hint: More readings alone are not enough here.

questions.learningObjective: Compute an attrition rate from wave counts
questions.stem: A travel survey starts with 1200 households and ends with 780 completed returns; what percentage of the starting households dropped out?
questions.explanation: Four hundred and twenty households are missing, and 420 over 1200 is 35 percent. The completion rate is the complement, 65 percent; reporting both shows how much the composition could have shifted.
questions.hint: Missing households over starting households.

questions.learningObjective: Order steps that keep selection from skewing a survey
questions.stem: A city wants to survey residents about a proposed tower; put the steps in the order that keeps selection from skewing the results.

options.text: Draw a random sample of households from the register, invite them with repeated attempts, then compare respondents with the register.
Post the survey on the tower's own website, then weight the results by the number of visits to the page.
options.misconception: Treats web traffic as a substitute for a probability sample

options.text: Survey the neighbours who attend the public meeting, since they are the people most affected by the tower.
options.misconception: Assumes the most affected are a representative sample

options.text: Survey residents of the three nearest streets first, then extend to other streets if the first results look clear.
options.misconception: Uses convenient streets as though they were random ones

questions.explanation: A random draw from the register, persistent invitation and a comparison with the register expose who declined. Website visitors, meeting attendees and nearby streets all select on views about the tower.
questions.hint: Random draw, then chase, then compare.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the history problem in a consultation window

stimulus.body: Extract from a parking consultation memo. Comment period opened on 3 May and closed on 14 June. Over the same period the council introduced a temporary suspension of parking charges on one side of the city, and a major employer moved its office to a nearby town. The memo reports 420 comments received, with sentiment noted as strongly opposed.

questions.stem: In the parking memo above, which statement best describes the history problem in this consultation?

options.text: The suspension and the office move occurred during the window, so comment volume and sentiment reflect world events.
The consultation is sound, because a six-week comment period is long enough to attract a representative sample.
options.misconception: Believes a longer window protects against coincident events

options.text: The only issue is the response rate, since 420 comments from a city of this size is a small number.
options.misconception: Reduces the problem to response volume rather than timing

options.text: The sentiment is inflated because the council ran the parking suspension without consulting residents first.
options.misconception: Links sentiment to the council's procedure rather than events

questions.explanation: A history effect means outside events coincided with the measurement period. The suspension and the office move fall inside the window, so comment volume and sentiment may reflect them, not the proposal.
questions.hint: Ask what else happened during the window.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the comparison needed to estimate maturation
questions.stem: A council measures residents' satisfaction with policing at the start and end of a two-year programme in two similar districts. Which step comes first?

options.text: Measure a comparable district with no programme over the same two years to estimate change that occurs anyway.
Measure the same residents again at the end and treat the difference as the programme's effect.
options.misconception: Relies on the same group without a comparison trajectory

options.text: Compare the two districts at the end date only, since their conditions are described as similar.
options.misconception: Measures only the endpoint and loses the baseline

options.text: Compare the two districts at the start date and assume that similarity guarantees equal change.
options.misconception: Treats matching baselines as proof of matching trends

questions.explanation: Maturation is change over time that happens anyway, so a comparison district is needed to estimate it before crediting differences to the programme. Endpoint-only comparisons leave maturation in the result.
questions.hint: Estimate the trend you would expect anyway.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a wave-to-wave change for testing effects
questions.stem: A city asks about wellbeing in a baseline survey and again in the follow-up, and wellbeing scores are lower in the follow-up wave.

options.text: Taking the same survey twice can itself lower scores, so the follow-up reflects exposure as well as any real change.
The lower scores prove the follow-up respondents were more honest than the baseline respondents.
options.misconception: Explains a testing effect through honesty rather than exposure

options.text: The lower scores cannot come from the survey because repeated questioning has no effect on answers.
options.misconception: Denies that repeated questioning can affect answers

options.text: The lower scores show the programme failed, since no wellbeing measure survives two waves of data.
options.misconception: Treats any wave-to-wave drop as programme failure

questions.explanation: Testing effects occur when the measurement influences later responses, common with wellbeing items. A drop between waves therefore mixes real change with the effect of having answered the questions before.
questions.hint: The questionnaire may be part of the cause.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a follow-up fall in a selected group
questions.stem: A support scheme targets residents whose waiting times were in the worst 10 percent last year; this year the average wait fell by 12 days.

options.text: The fall is partly regression to the mean, because the group was selected on an extreme value.
The fall is a clean estimate of the scheme, because the same group was followed consistently.
options.misconception: Ignores the selection on an extreme baseline value

options.text: The fall must be caused by the scheme, since waiting times rarely change without intervention.
options.misconception: Assumes spontaneous change in waiting times is rare

options.text: The fall is too small to be meaningful, because 12 days is well under a month.
options.misconception: Judges the change by magnitude rather than design

questions.explanation: Selecting the worst 10 percent on a noisy measure guarantees partial reversion, so part of the 12 day fall is expected without the scheme. Consistent follow-up and a plausible size do not remove that.
questions.hint: The group was chosen because it looked extreme.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between cause and extension
questions.stem: A pilot of a street greening scheme ran for one summer in a low-traffic residential street, and the memo calls it a city-wide success.

answer.exemplar: The pilot shows that greening was delivered and that residents on that street responded positively at that time, which is a causal claim about one place and one season. Calling it a city-wide success extends the finding to traffic, soils, budgets and resident expectations that differ widely across the city, and it also ignores how a single summer's weather and the short follow-up period shape the result.

questions.explanation: Internal validity concerns cause in the pilot setting and external validity whether the finding extends to other places and times. One quiet street in one summer says little about busy commercial streets in other seasons.
questions.hint: Separate what it shows from what it claims.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a percentage reduction from two counts
questions.stem: A before-and-after count of pedestrian injuries shows 24 in the year before a crossing change and 18 after; what percentage reduction does this represent?
questions.explanation: The reduction is 24 minus 18, which is 6, and 6 over 24 is 25 percent. The arithmetic is right, but without a control site a before-and-after comparison cannot show the change caused the drop.
questions.hint: Compare the drop with the starting count.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order steps that handle withdrawals transparently
questions.stem: A resident survey runs three waves; put the steps in the order that handles withdrawals without hiding them.

options.text: Record who responds at each wave, compare waves on those present throughout, and report the withdrawals alongside.
Report the final wave only, since it contains the most complete picture of current opinion.
options.misconception: Reports the final wave as if it represented everyone

options.text: Replace withdrawn respondents with new recruits at each wave, then analyse all responses as one sample.
options.misconception: Patches withdrawals by adding people mid-study

options.text: Drop the first wave from the analysis so that all remaining waves share the same composition.
options.misconception: Deletes the wave that reveals the composition change

questions.explanation: Attrition is handled by measuring it: record who responded, compare on respondents present throughout, and publish the withdrawal pattern. Using only the final wave or replacing leavers hides the problem.
questions.hint: Show who stayed and who left.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose selection in a volunteered consultation

stimulus.body: Extract from a leisure centre memo. The consultation was advertised on social media, in the centre's foyer and on a local radio slot. Respondents were asked to rate current facilities. The memo reports 512 responses, 68 percent of them saying they would use a new sauna, and notes that 140 people signed the paper list in the foyer on the two busiest evenings.

questions.stem: In the leisure centre memo above, which statement best describes the selection problem in this consultation?

options.text: People with a strong view were more likely to respond, so the sauna support figure reflects the motivated.
The consultation is unbiased, because 512 responses is a substantial number for a centre of this size.
options.misconception: Treats a large response count as evidence of representativeness

options.text: The sauna figure is reliable, because the foyer list shows that a broad cross-section attended.
options.misconception: Treats a convenience list as a cross-section of residents

options.text: The problem is only the missing budget detail, since recruitment drives how many responded.
options.misconception: Redirects the issue to documentation rather than who responded

questions.explanation: Selection bias arises when the chance of responding depends on the answer. People with an opinion are likelier to reply, so the figure describes the motivated, whatever the total count.
questions.hint: Ask who was likely to answer at all.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the check needed when two changes coincide
questions.stem: A memo credits a waste collection change with a drop in fly-tipping, but the city also increased enforcement that month. Which step comes first?

options.text: Establish whether the enforcement change alone accounts for the drop, using comparable unaffected areas and timing.
Publish the finding now, since the waste change was implemented on the first of the month as planned.
options.misconception: Publishes before checking the competing explanation

options.text: Attribute the drop to whichever change residents mentioned more often in their complaints.
options.misconception: Chooses the explanation by mention frequency alone

options.text: Remove the enforcement from the memo's background section so that only one change appears to be under test.
options.misconception: Conceals the competing treatment instead of testing it

questions.explanation: Two changes moved together, so the memo must first establish which produced the drop, using areas not subject to enforcement and timing that separates them. Choosing by complaint frequency avoids the question.
questions.hint: Two changes moved together, so separate them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify maturation in a two-year programme
questions.stem: A two-year skills programme measures confidence in job interviews; participants naturally grow more confident over two years regardless of the course.

options.text: This natural growth is maturation, so the course's contribution needs a comparison group measured over the same period.
This natural growth means the confidence measure is invalid, since change over time cannot be detected.
options.misconception: Blames the measure for a real change over time

options.text: This natural growth is a history effect, because the economy changed during the two years.
options.misconception: Calls ordinary development a coinciding outside event

options.text: This natural growth is regression to the mean, because participants started with low confidence.
options.misconception: Confuses natural growth with reversion to the average

questions.explanation: Maturation is development that occurs over time anyway, and a comparison group on the same dates estimates it. Growth regardless of the course is not the course's effect, and it is not reversion.
questions.hint: Development over time, with or without the course.

questions.learningObjective: Read a repeat-survey pattern for testing effects
questions.stem: A survey on park use is completed twice a year; scores for parks surveyed in year one fall in year two compared with parks first surveyed in year two.

options.text: Parks surveyed twice show a decline that repeat questioning alone can explain, so the drop is not a clean trend.
The pattern shows a real decline in park use, because twice-yearly surveys catch more change than annual ones.
options.misconception: Reads a testing pattern as a substantive decline

options.text: The pattern is irrelevant, because the same parks must show the same results each time they are asked.
options.misconception: Expects identical results from repeated questions

options.text: The pattern shows the year-two first-time parks are unrepresentative, since they score higher for no clear reason.
options.misconception: Explains the pattern as unrepresentativeness

questions.explanation: Parks that answered twice are exposed to the testing effect, so their fall can reflect the repeated survey, not a real decline. Comparing with parks surveyed once reveals that contamination.
questions.hint: Which parks were asked twice?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain reversion in a targeted group
questions.stem: A performance rating scheme gives extra mentoring to the bottom-rated officers, and their ratings improve the following year.

answer.exemplar: Bottom-rated officers were selected partly because their first rating reflected a hard posting, an unfamiliar assessor or simply a noisy week, and extreme ratings are followed by less extreme ones. Because the scheme gives support to exactly the people most likely to improve anyway, the observed improvement cannot be read as the effect of the mentoring without a comparable group of low-rated officers who did not receive it.

questions.explanation: Regression to the mean means extreme ratings are followed by less extreme ones, and the scheme targeted that group. Without a comparable low-rated group left untreated, the improvement cannot be credited to mentoring.
questions.hint: The group was chosen because it looked worst.

options.misconception: Concludes no conclusion is possible from the data

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a history event in a quarterly comparison
questions.stem: A memo about a new bus lane notes that congestion fell in the quarter after the lane opened, but the fuel price also fell that quarter.

options.text: The fuel price change is a history event, so the congestion fall cannot be credited to the lane alone.
The fuel price change strengthens the finding, because two independent causes produced the same result.
options.misconception: Treats a coinciding event as confirming the intervention

options.text: The fuel price change is irrelevant, since fuel prices affect drivers rather than buses.
options.misconception: Excludes drivers from the population the lane affects

options.text: The congestion fall is a regression to the mean, because congestion was high before the lane opened.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated survey waves need a fresh comparison
questions.stem: A council's repeated resident survey asks about satisfaction with services at every wave, and satisfaction scores fall each time.

answer.exemplar: Repeated administration of the same satisfaction items can itself lower reported satisfaction, because respondents grow tired of the topic, notice the questions again and infer that something must have changed. The way to separate the two is to add a group asked only once at the final wave and compare that group with the repeatedly asked ones.

questions.explanation: Every wave in a repeat survey is exposed to the questionnaire, so declining scores may reflect testing rather than services. A group asked only at the final wave provides the unexposed comparison.

questions.learningObjective: Explain maturation in a confidence measure
questions.stem: A two-year training programme for new council officers reports that average confidence scores rose each quarter.

answer.exemplar: Confidence in one's own role tends to build with time on the job regardless of any programme, which is maturation and would be visible in new officers who received nothing. questions.explanation: Maturation is confidence that builds with time on the job, and participants alone cannot separate it from programme effects. A comparable group of new officers measured on the same schedule estimates the ordinary development.

options.text: The block had unusually high fault volumes, so the result may not describe typical blocks or typical households.
The generalisation is sound, because the block was selected on a measured administrative variable.
options.misconception: Treats objective selection as representative selection

options.text: The generalisation is sound, because the outcome, repair time, is measured in the same way for everyone.
options.misconception: Believes uniform measurement removes the sampling issue

options.misconception: Summarises the same uncontrolled comparison in another way

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify selective reporting in a set of evaluations
questions.stem: A council runs 40 separate scheme evaluations; 12 of them report a positive effect, and the memo cites the 12 as evidence the programme works.

options.text: Selecting the 12 positive results from 40 evaluations and reporting them alone is selective reporting, not evidence.
The 12 positive results out of 40 are a clear majority, so the programme is evidently effective.
options.misconception: Compares a subgroup with a whole and calls it a majority

options.text: The 12 results are the strongest available evidence, since weak studies are less likely to be published.
options.misconception: Justifies selective reporting with a publication argument

options.text: The 12 results show that the programme works where it is implemented well, which is what matters.
options.misconception: Recasts selective reporting as a condition of success

questions.explanation: Citing only positive results from 40 evaluations is selective reporting, and the reader cannot see the base rate of findings. Validity requires the full set or a pre-specified selection rule.
questions.hint: Ask how many evaluations were not cited.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a fixed panel does and does not cover
questions.stem: A consultation on a park renewal keeps the same 300 residents across two rounds, and the memo reports that support for the scheme fell between rounds.

answer.exemplar: Holding the same people across both rounds removes compositional change between waves, so the fall in support is a change in the same respondents' views rather than a swap in who was asked. That is a cleaner comparison than one built on different samples each round, and it is exactly what makes the fall interpretable, though it also means the findings describe those 300 continuing residents rather than all residents of the area.

questions.explanation: Keeping the same respondents removes composition change between rounds, so the fall reflects changed views rather than a different group answering. The cost is that findings describe only the 300 who continued.
questions.hint: Same people in both rounds limits who is covered.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a response rate against the drawn sample
questions.stem: A city survey draws 500 households from a register of 2000 and receives 320 completed forms; what percentage of the drawn households actually responded?
questions.explanation: Three hundred and twenty of five hundred drawn households responded, which is 64 percent. Whether those responders resemble the register is separate, since many refusals can leave a biased set.
questions.hint: Respondents divided by all households drawn.
